mainEntity.name: How much does a 6-foot wood fence cost per linear foot in Oakland County?

acceptedAnswer.text: Eastern white cedar runs $34 to $44 per linear foot installed and pressure-treated pine runs $26 to $34 for a standard dog-ear privacy build on level ground with good access. Board-on-board western red cedar runs $44 to $58. Gates, old-fence removal, permits and staining are priced separately and typically add 15 to 25 percent to the total.

mainEntity.name: Is cedar worth the extra cost over pressure-treated pine in Michigan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually yes if you are staying in the house more than eight years. Treated pine costs roughly $8 per foot less installed but moves more through freeze-thaw cycles and needs its first finish sooner. Cedar's natural rot resistance holds up longer through wet-dry cycling and takes repairs invisibly. If you plan to sell within three years, pine is the rational buy.

mainEntity.name: Does removing the old fence cost extra?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Removal runs about $3 to $5 per linear foot, or $480 to $800 on a 160-foot run, including hauling and disposal. It is frequently left out of a low bid, which is one reason two quotes for the same fence can differ by several hundred dollars before anything else is compared.

mainEntity.name: How much does a gate add to a fence?

acceptedAnswer.text: A four-foot cedar walk gate runs about $450 to $900 installed. A five-foot double drive gate runs $1,100 to $2,600. Cost depends on frame construction, hinge count, hardware quality, and whether the gate must be self-closing or self-latching. Count the gates in each bid before comparing totals.

mainEntity.name: Do I need a permit for a fence in Oakland County, and who pulls it?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most Oakland County communities require a fence permit, typically $50 to $250 with a one-to-two-week review; Rochester Hills publishes a $50 to $175 band. The contractor is responsible for obtaining required permits, and a Michigan residential contract above $600 must state that. Height limits and setback lines differ by municipality, so confirm your city's rules first.

mainEntity.name: What deposit should I pay a fence contractor in Michigan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Michigan sets no statewide cap on deposits, so treat it as a negotiation. A deposit covering materials and mobilization is normal; paying the full job up front is not, and LARA's homeowner guidance says never to do it. Pay by check to the company name, get a receipt, and tie progress payments to completed milestones.

mainEntity.name: Is it cheaper to have a fence installed in winter?

acceptedAnswer.text: Often by 5 to 10 percent, and scheduling is faster because the spring backlog has not formed. Frozen ground changes how holes are dug but does not prevent installation. The one step that must wait is staining and sealing, which needs sustained temperatures above roughly 50 degrees Fahrenheit, so the finish usually happens the following spring.

mainEntity.name: How much does it cost to stain a new wood fence, and how often?

acceptedAnswer.text: About $1.50 to $3.00 per linear foot per application, or $240 to $480 on a 160-foot fence, every two to three years. A new cedar fence should get its first finish within six to twelve months once the wood has dried, then on a two-to-three-year cycle. Skipping it does not save the money; it moves the cost to board replacement.
